title: Root-system structure of sloppiness in passive Gaussian metrology
abstract: Passive transformations of an $n$-mode squeezed probe become locally unidentifiable when the quantum Fisher matrix loses rank. For pure zero-mean Gaussian probes, we show that the $C_{n}$ restricted-root system of $\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{U}(n)$ governs this exact sloppiness. For squeezing magnitudes $r_{1},\ldots,r_{n}$ in the canonical basis, the roots $2r_{j}$ and $r_{j}\pm r_{k}$ label the local phase rotations and two beam-splitter quadratures, and their vanishing identifies every Fisher-null direction. The associated Fisher weights quantify the approach to each singular wall. At fixed positive mean photon number, we solve the E-optimal probe-design problem of maximizing the smallest passive Fisher eigenvalue in two explicit generator normalizations. In the canonical phase and beam-splitter angle convention, the unique optimum in the fundamental Weyl chamber is an arithmetic progression approaching the consecutive-odd-integer dual-Weyl direction at large resource. With an invariant generator norm, the smallest eigenvalue is independent of the passive frame and the optimum lies exactly on that ray at every resource. Uniform squeezing instead minimizes the local-phase A-optimal cost while leaving one beam-splitter quadrature unidentifiable for every mode pair. Finally, the two quadratures of each identifiable mode pair saturate the quantum-geometric incompatibility bound, and the largest compatible passive submodel has $n(n+1)/2$ parameters at a regular spectrum. The resulting classification separates local identifiability, sensitivity optimization, and simultaneous attainability.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes the fundamental limits of quantum sensing using passive Gaussian transformations. It shows that the loss of measurement identifiability is governed by the $C_n$ root system, and it derives optimal squeezing strategies for maximizing measurement sensitivity. The results provide a comprehensive classification of local identifiability, sensitivity optimization, and resource compatibility in quantum metrology.
main_problem: The paper determines the global structure governing parameter identifiability, sensitivity, and compatibility for passive Gaussian transformations in quantum metrology.
main_result: The exact sloppiness structure is governed by the $C_n$ restricted-root system, and the E-optimal probe design leads to an arithmetic progression for the optimal squeezing spectrum.
method: The authors use algebraic geometry (restricted-root systems) combined with quantum estimation theory (Quantum Fisher Matrix analysis) to map physical limitations to mathematical structures.
model_or_system: The system involves $n$-mode squeezed Gaussian probes undergoing passive transformations, analyzed within the framework of the Lie group $	ext{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})/	ext{U}(n)$.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Matrix (QFI) eigenvalues, passive Fisher weights, and the condition number ($\kappa$) of the sensitivity matrix.
important_parameters: Squeezing spectrum $r = (r_1, \dots, r_n)$, mean photon number $N$, and the resource allocation parameter $a$.
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on pure zero-mean Gaussian probes and utilizes the canonical squeezing basis for initial structural identification.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the restricted-root arrangements for $C_2$ and $C_3$, showing singular lines/planes corresponding to vanishing Fisher weights, and compare optimal design strategies.
paper_structure: The paper systematically moves from identifying the algebraic structure ($C_n$ roots) governing Fisher-rank loss, to solving optimization problems (E-optimal, A-optimal) for probe design, and finally analyzing resource limits and degeneracy lifting via displacement measurements.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep mathematical framework connecting the algebraic structure of symmetry groups (root systems) directly to the fundamental physical limits of quantum measurement precision in continuous variable systems.
